claims.text: Multiplexing DSC measurements across an array of HEA compositions enables efficient, high-throughput characterization.
A platform combining DSC, high-temperature volume measurements, and CALPHAD screening can accurately characterize a broad range of HEAs.
Rapid melting and solidification can produce homogeneous, single-phase HEA solid solutions suitable for the proposed measurements.
CALPHAD pre-screening can identify HEAs that melt within the measurable temperature range and exhibit simple, single-phase melting behavior.
Single-phase FCC or BCC HEA solid solutions produce one well-defined melting event without interference from other phase transitions.
DSC detects a characteristic endothermic signal associated with melting.
The onset and peak of the DSC melting signal determine melting temperatures.
The DSC melting signal can be used to determine the latent enthalpy of fusion.
Dilatometry or in-situ high-temperature imaging captures the abrupt volume change at melting.
Fusion entropy can be calculated as ΔSf = ΔHf/Tm.
Combining calorimetry and volume measurements provides liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
Near-equimolar multicomponent mixing in HEAs produces a substantial configurational-entropy contribution.
Configurational entropy promotes a uniform solid phase in HEAs.
Configurational-entropy stabilization of a uniform phase leads to a distinct melting signature.
The multiplexed method will measure melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and melting volume change within ±5–10% of traditional single-sample measurements.
Clear and quantitatively reliable thermal signatures will be observed across the screened HEA composition range.
The approach performs best for HEAs that form single-phase solid solutions.
Phase segregation, multiple-step melting, disorder–order transitions, and minor second phases can reduce accuracy or prevent deconvolution of measured thermodynamic properties.
